steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey paper on causal discovery methods for both I.I.D. and time series data. Explain what causal discovery is and why it matters, how this survey differs from existing ones, and give an overview of the paper's structure.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Causal Discovery (CD) is the identification of the cause-effect relationships among the variables of a system from its data. A big part of causal analysis is uncovering the cause and effect relationships among the entities in complex systems, which can help us build better solutions in health care, earth science, politics, business, education and many other areas. The causal explanations, i.e. the causal factors we get from a causal analysis, are important in decision-making and policy formulation, and also in predicting the consequences of interventions without actually doing them. Causal discovery algorithms make it possible to discover the underlying causal structure from a set of observations. The underlying causal structure, also called a causal graph (CG), represents the cause-effect relationships between the variables in the data. Causal graphs show the causal relationships with directed arrows going from the cause to the effect.

If we discover the causal relations and so estimate their effects, we can understand the underlying data generating mechanism (DGM) better and take the necessary interventional actions. But traditional Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications only rely on predictive models and often ignore causal knowledge. Systems that do not know the causal relationships often cannot make rational and informed decisions. Mistaking correlations for causation can have devastating results. Two variables can be highly correlated and still not have any causal influence on each other. There may be a third variable, often called a latent confounder or hidden factor, that causes both of them (see Figure 2 (a)). So it is important to embed knowledge of causal relationships in black-box AI systems to make them more explainable and reliable. In many fields like healthcare, politics, economics, climate science, business and education, being able to understand causal relations can help formulate better policies with a better understanding of the data.

- RCTs vs. observational methods
  - RCTs infeasible (costs, ethics) -> observational methods based on assumptions
  - output causal graph / adjacency matrix, DAG-like; Figure 2 (b) Cancer example
- Gap and scope
  - I.I.D. vs. time series approaches; prior knowledge incorporation
  - existing surveys (Table 1) don't cover both or background knowledge
  - CI testing, score functions, FCMs, continuous optimization, prior knowledge, miscellaneous; tools, metrics, datasets, challenges, applications
- Paper structure
  - sections 2-10 overview

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Causal Discovery (CD) is the identification of the cause-effect relationships among the variables of a system from its data. A big part of causal analysis is uncovering the cause and effect relationships among the entities in complex systems, which can help us build better solutions in health care, earth science, politics, business, education and many other areas. The causal explanations, i.e. the causal factors we get from a causal analysis, are important in decision-making and policy formulation, and also in predicting the consequences of interventions without actually doing them. Causal discovery algorithms make it possible to discover the underlying causal structure from a set of observations. The underlying causal structure, also called a causal graph (CG), represents the cause-effect relationships between the variables in the data. Causal graphs show the causal relationships with directed arrows going from the cause to the effect.

If we discover the causal relations and so estimate their effects, we can understand the underlying data generating mechanism (DGM) better and take the necessary interventional actions. But traditional Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications only rely on predictive models and often ignore causal knowledge. Systems that do not know the causal relationships often cannot make rational and informed decisions. Mistaking correlations for causation can have devastating results. Two variables can be highly correlated and still not have any causal influence on each other. There may be a third variable, often called a latent confounder or hidden factor, that causes both of them (see Figure 2 (a)). So it is important to embed knowledge of causal relationships in black-box AI systems to make them more explainable and reliable. In many fields like healthcare, politics, economics, climate science, business and education, being able to understand causal relations can help formulate better policies with a better understanding of the data.

The standard way to discover cause-effect relationships is to do randomized control trials (RCTs). But RCTs are often not feasible because of high costs and some ethical reasons. Because of this, in the last few decades researchers have developed a variety of methods to find causal relations from purely observational data. These methods are often based on some assumptions about the data and the underlying mechanism. Any causal discovery method outputs a causal graph or a causal adjacency matrix that represents the cause and effect relations among the entities or variables. The structure of a causal graph is often like a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where directed edges from one variable to another represent the cause-effect relationship between them. Figure 2 (b) shows a causal graph with the factors that are responsible for causing Cancer. This kind of structural representation of the data-generating mechanism helps us understand how the entities of the system interact with each other.

There are many approaches for causal discovery under different settings or assumptions. Some are designed especially for independent and identically distributed (I.I.D.) data, i.e. non-temporal data, and others focus on time series data, i.e. temporal data. In real-world settings both types of data exist in different problem domains, so we need approaches that can recover causal structure from both. Recently there is also a growing body of research that incorporates prior knowledge to recover causal relationships. There are some surveys (see Table 1) on causal discovery approaches, but none of them gives a comprehensive review of the approaches for structure recovery from both I.I.D. and time series data. These surveys also do not discuss approaches that do causal discovery when background knowledge is available. So the goal of this survey is to give an overview of the wide range of existing approaches for causal discovery from I.I.D. as well as time series data under different settings. Existing surveys do not have a combined overview of the approaches for both I.I.D. and time series data, so in this survey we want to introduce readers to the methods in both domains. We discuss prominent methods based on different approaches: conditional independence (CI) testing, using a score function, functional causal models (FCMs), continuous optimization, infusing prior knowledge, and miscellaneous ones. The methods mainly differ in the primary strategy they follow. Besides introducing the causal discovery approaches and algorithms for I.I.D. and time series data, we also discuss the tools, metrics and benchmark datasets used for CD, and the challenges and applications of CD in many areas.

The structure of this paper is as follows. First, we briefly introduce the common terminology in causal discovery (section 2). Second, we discuss the causal discovery approaches for I.I.D. data (section 3) and time-series data (section 4). Third, we give a short overview of the common evaluation metrics (section 5) and datasets (section 6) for evaluating causal discovery approaches, and we report a performance comparison of some approaches in section 7. Fourth, we list the technologies and open-source software (section 8) available for causal discovery. Fifth, we discuss the challenges (section 9.1) and applications (section 9.2) of causal discovery in areas like healthcare, business, social science, economics and so on. Finally, we conclude by discussing what can be improved in future causal discovery research, and why causality is important for improving existing predictive AI systems, which can affect informed and reliable decision-making in different areas (section 10).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The identification of the cause-effect relationships among the variables of a system from the corresponding data is called Causal Discovery (CD). A major part of causal analysis involves unfolding the cause and effect relationships among the entities in complex systems, which can help us build better solutions in health care, earth science, politics, business, education, and many other diverse areas ([1], [2]). The causal explanations, precisely the causal factors obtained from a causal analysis, play an important role in decision-making and policy formulation as well as in foreseeing the consequences of interventions without actually performing them. Causal discovery algorithms enable the discovery of the underlying causal structure given a set of observations. The underlying causal structure, also known as a causal graph (CG), is a representation of the cause-effect relationships between the variables in the data ([3]). Causal graphs represent causal relationships with directed arrows from the cause to the effect.

Discovering the causal relations, and thereby estimating their effects, would enable us to better understand the underlying data generating mechanism (DGM) and take the necessary interventional actions. However, traditional Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications rely solely on predictive models and often ignore causal knowledge. Systems without knowledge of causal relationships often cannot make rational and informed decisions ([4]). The result may be devastating when correlations are mistaken for causation, because two variables can be highly correlated and yet not have any causal influence on each other. There may be a third variable, often called a latent confounder or hidden factor, that causes both of them (see Figure 2 (a)). Thus, embedding knowledge of causal relationships in black-box AI systems is important to improve their explainability and reliability ([5], [6]). In fields such as healthcare, politics, economics, climate science, business, and education, the ability to understand causal relations can facilitate the formulation of better policies with a greater understanding of the data.

The standard approach to discovering cause-effect relationships is to perform randomized control trials (RCTs) ([8]). However, RCTs are often infeasible due to high costs and ethical reasons ([9]). As a result, over the last few decades researchers have developed a variety of methods to unravel causal relations from purely observational data ([10], [11]). These methods are often based on some assumptions about the data and the underlying mechanism. The outcome of any causal discovery method is a causal graph or a causal adjacency matrix in which the cause and effect relations among the entities or variables are represented. The structure of a causal graph is often similar to a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where directed edges from one variable to another represent the cause-effect relationship between them. Figure 2 (b) shows a causal graph of the factors responsible for causing Cancer. This type of structural representation of the underlying data-generating mechanism is useful for understanding how the system entities interact with each other.

There exists a wide range of approaches for performing causal discovery under different settings or assumptions. Some are designed particularly for independent and identically distributed (I.I.D.) data ([12], [13]), i.e. non-temporal data, while others focus on time series data ([14], [15]), i.e. temporal data. Since both types of data are available in different real-world problem domains, it is essential to have approaches for causal structure recovery from both. Recently, there has been a growing body of research that incorporates prior knowledge for recovering causal relationships ([16], [17], [18]). Although there exist some surveys (see Table 1) on causal discovery approaches ([19], [10], [20], [11], [21]), none of them presents a comprehensive review of the approaches designed for structure recovery from both I.I.D. and time series data. These surveys also do not discuss approaches that perform causal discovery in the presence of background knowledge. Hence, the goal of this survey is to provide an overview of the wide range of existing approaches for causal discovery from I.I.D. as well as time series data under different settings. Since existing surveys lack a combined overview of the approaches for both I.I.D. and time series data, in this survey we want to introduce readers to the methods available in both domains. We discuss prominent methods based on different approaches such as conditional independence (CI) testing, score function usage, functional causal models (FCMs), continuous optimization strategies, prior knowledge infusion, and miscellaneous ones. These methods differ from each other mainly in the primary strategy they follow. Apart from introducing the different causal discovery approaches and algorithms for I.I.D. and time series data, we also discuss the tools, metrics, and benchmark datasets used for performing CD, as well as the challenges and applications of CD in a wide range of areas.

To summarize, the structure of this paper is as follows. First, we briefly introduce the common terminology in the field of causal discovery (section 2). Second, we discuss the range of causal discovery approaches for I.I.D. (section 3) and time-series data (section 4). Third, we briefly overview the common evaluation metrics (section 5) and datasets (section 6) used for evaluating causal discovery approaches, and report a performance comparison of some approaches in section 7. Fourth, we list the technologies and open-source software (section 8) available for performing causal discovery. Fifth, we discuss the challenges (section 9.1) and applications (section 9.2) of causal discovery in areas such as healthcare, business, social science, economics, and so on. Lastly, we conclude by discussing the scope for improvement in future causal discovery research, and the importance of causality in improving existing predictive AI systems, which can impact informed and reliable decision-making in different areas of interest (section 10).
